utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to deal yesterday with the theme, as it were, of religious and cultural destruction and destruction of property that took place in this area during the period that Your Honours will be considering. If Your Honours have in front of you now on the screen a map -- again, I'm afraid it really -- it was there and it's gone again on my screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you speak into the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The map was there, but it seems to have gone again. Obviously, me and the technological miracles of this Court are not compatible. However, Your Honours, again, it sets out in form the places where religious destruction took place. I said yesterday that it is the Prosecution's case that it wasn't enough simply to drive out the non-Serb population. The attempt -- the objective of the Bosnian Serbs was to try and ensure that they never came back to the area, and in order to do that, they had to destroy their homes but, almost more importantly, any traces of their culture or religion. The number of damaged or destroyed mosques -- and may I say that I'm using mosques as a generic term. Your Honours will be hearing from an expert who will explain to you that a mosque is a particular type of Muslim building. There are other proper words to describe smaller religious institutions but I'm just using it as a generic term. Your Honour, we listed the majority of the mosques and religious -- and Roman Catholic churches in paragraph 47(b) of the indictment. I have to say that it is not an exhaustive list. Your Honours will be hearing about other damaged mosques which simply fell through the net. These religious buildings were destroyed or damaged, both by shelling during attacks, and by the setting of explosions, the use of mines and the like and grenades. When destruction took place through the use of explosives, this was usually at night and it is rare that any witness is able to give more of a description of the people who caused the explosions than to say they were men in uniform. But in many cases, the destruction was extremely skillful and therefore it is suggested that the persons who were doing the deed were familiar with explosives. Of all the municipalities that we will be dealing with in this case, really only Banja Luka in 1992 escaped serious damage or destruction to the -- its mosques. The most famous mosque, the Ferhadija mosque which was the subject of so much trouble last year, was in fact damaged and virtually destroyed in 1993, not 1992. In fact, as Your Honours will hear, Banja Luka is virtually an exception to all the municipalities for a reason that we will suggest later on. The municipalities with the highest total of damaged or destroyed mosques and churches were Prijedor and Sanski Most. In nearly all of the events, these two municipalities figure high on the list. The Prosecution suggest that the period of intensive destruction of mosques that Your Honours will hear about was between roughly May and October of 1992. There were fewer Roman Catholic churches and religious buildings damaged or destroyed simply because there were fewer buildings. And as we've already pointed out, the Croats were a much smaller proportion of the population in this area than the Muslims. However, if one looks at the overall picture, the appearance, we suggest, is that of a deliberate campaign of devastation, not accidental, not the sort of thing that would happen because a village was being fired upon or that there was fighting going on. We suggest that this was deliberate targeted destruction. We suggest that it would be impossible for anyone who was in that area at that time, let alone persons in authority, not to have realised what was happening. In fact, numerous people brought it to the attention of General Talic, not least the bishop of Banja Luka, Bishop Komarica, who in fact wrote a book publishing the letters that he had written to the various people in charge, complaining about what was happening not only to religious buildings but also to Catholic priests and the like. And as a result, no doubt because of this pressure, on the 23rd of June, 1992, General Talic issued an order. And I wonder if we could have that put up on the ELMO, please, so that Your Honours could see this. It is a document, disclosure number 4.646. Your Honour will see that it is headed "The 1st Krajina Corps Command," dated the 23rd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, it hasn't appeared on your screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours will see "1st Krajina Corps Command." And if we could draw back for a moment. Thank you. "Preventing the desecration of religious buildings. Order. In accordance with the views of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Army Main Staff, and in order to provide guidance for members of the 1st KK, Krajina Corps, so that they continue fighting the war in a military and honourable manner, I hereby order, ensure at all levels of command that religious buildings or cemeteries of any religion are not desecrated in combat operations or any other situations. 2. In combat operations, fire may be opened on religious buildings only when our forces are being engaged from such buildings or when it has been determined that they house an armed enemy who refuses to surrender. The intensity of fire and the type of weapons used should be such as to destroy or neutralise only enemy personnel, without destroying the building. In this connection, members of the Corps are hereby informed that the SR BH Army will fight the war against the enemy in a military and honourable manner, consistently abiding by the provisions of the Geneva Convention. 3. I hereby forbid harassment or maltreatment of clerics. Such persons who are known or suspected of being on the side of the enemy should be arrested and taken into custody by the military police..." Can you just slow down for a moment. "...security service, or Ministry of the Interior organs. The civilian population should be treated in the same manner. I shall hold all unit commanders, also all Corps members, responsible for consistent execution of this order." "To achieve this" -- and this is in his handwriting -- "unit commanders shall ensure that this order reaches every single individual." And it's signed commander Major General Momir Talic. And as far as I'm aware, there's no dispute that this was an order actually signed by General Talic. Your Honour, on the 3rd of August - that order was in June - at the same time as he was issuing - that is, General Talic - instructions, you will recall, to clean up the camps in anticipation of the visit of the international persons and the media, he issued a second order in respect of places of worship. I actually thought I was going rather slowly. Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Actually, I thought it was addressed to me, because you're definitely going slow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's probably when one is reading a document, we tend to speed up. I wonder if that document could now be put up, please, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is dated the 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the same day the order was issued in respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when there's a reference to order number 536-2 of 23rd June, it's specifically referring to the one we've just seen before this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you will see, as Your Honours have already read, despite the order with the number of 23rd of June, 1992, we are still witnessing instances of demolition of places of worship. "We warn all unit commanders to prevent such irresponsible acts. Failure to abide by my order represents a criminal act and shall be dealt with accordingly. You are required to submit a detailed report and an explanation whenever a place of worship is demolished." And obviously a copy of the order was enclosed. I should add -- it's not on Your Honour's screen, but attached to both orders is a list, a distribution list, to the various units to which it was sent. Now, the motive behind these orders, the timing of these orders is a matter that Your Honours will have to decide on when listening to the evidence. What is absolutely clear from that evidence is, despite those two public orders, the destruction continued and no action seemed to have been taken in respect of the persons who were committing that destruction. It wasn't only the military who had the matter brought to their attention. In Teslic, a report was issued by the public prosecutor on what had happened in Teslic between June and September, 1992. It would appear that these reports were a regular part of the duties of public prosecutors who had to submit reports on activities on a regular basis. I'm going to ask that part of that report be placed, again, on the ELMO. If Your Honours look at the first paragraph, it states this: "The destruction of religious buildings is a war crime against civilians because of the way and circumstances in which it was perpetrated. The Serbian people will carry a heavy burden of historical responsibility until the perpetrators of these and similar criminal acts are brought to justice." If we could go back just to the previous page, although it's slightly off the point -- perhaps I could hand it in. Your Honour, for the purposes of Defence counsel, this document was disclosed as 4.285. That part of the report that I just looked at with Your Honours is actually part of a paragraph headed "Actual Crime Situation." "Recorded crime is a fraction of the real crime existing in society today. Most criminal acts remain undiscovered, and many crimes are tolerated by the authorities for various reasons. The Prosecutor's Office has knowledge of the day-to-day looting of property, houses and business premises being set on fire and destroyed, armed robbery and murder being committed for base motives, socially owned flats and private houses being occupied unlawfully." I omit the next part. "There is no criminal prosecution for most of these acts. In ten days alone, there were three murders for base motives and several cases of arson and armed robbery. In only one case were the perpetrators arrested and criminal proceedings initiated against them. The perpetrators of the other two murders have not been arrested to the present day. The public prosecutor and the president of the court personally demanded that the command of the Teslic Serbian Brigade arrest one accomplice on suspicion of murder. It is inexplicable why these people have not been arrested." Your Honour, Teslic came under the area of responsibility of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, Madam Prosecutor, when we are referring to an exhibit that has been summarised by Madam Korner, we see that it is drafted in Serbo-Croat. We notice that it is a document that doesn't have a heading, no stamp, no signature, drafted on white paper, and we contest its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's something that will -- we will come to later on, but for the purposes of the opening statement, we are adopting the same procedure we adopted yesterday: Everything will be done without prejudice to problems such as the one you just mentioned now. In any case, this is a document which has been disclosed and you have been given the reference number, so we will be able to deal with that later. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution suggest that it is not inexplicable, that a deliberate policy was taken by the military and civilian authorities not to prosecute for these type of crimes, particularly when committed against non-Serbs. The destruction of housing and property belonging to non-Serbs was far greater. It's almost incalculable how much was destroyed. The destruction can still be seen by those who travel to Bosnia today, the programme of rebuilding notwithstanding. That it was targeted destruction - particularly when it was not caused by shelling or attacks but by persons blowing up those houses, or in some way destroying them by fire, nearly always after looting and after the population had been removed - becomes extremely obvious in the areas where the villages or towns were mixed, in other words there were Serb population, Serb churches -- Orthodox churches, and those belonging to non-Serbs. Your Honour, this was very clearly shown in a broadcast made by ABC news, in a programme called "Nightline" in November of 1992 when the reporter visited the town of Kozarac in the Prijedor municipality. Your Honour, I'm going to ask that a short clip be shown. May I say that the reporter talks about ethnic cleansing. Of course, as with newspapers we all know that reporters are there to take news and we do not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rely on obviously what the reporter himself says. It's the pictures we'd like Your Honour to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Reporter: "... come from the same village in northern Bosnia, an area dominated by two cities, Prijedor and Banja Luka, and a once-thriving Muslim town called Kozarac. We visited the ethnically cleansed Kozarac in northern Bosnia last week. We were closely supervised by the local Serb militia, restricted to just a few blocks of the town once home to about 15.000, men, women and children. Today, there are no Muslims there, none, and none of their X-marked homes is intact. Other homes in Kozarac have been marked "To survive," this one with the colours of the Serbian flag. This one says, "This is Serbia." They stand undamaged, like the remaining Serb residents of Kozarac, surrounded in silence, deadly silence."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, what that reporter saw there in November, 1992, was exactly like that in the early part of 1996 when the area was first visited by representatives of this Tribunal. Your Honours, can I now turn to the topic of the killings, about which Your Honours will hear evidence? The major killings in this case are set out in paragraphs 38 and 41 of this indictment. When I say "major killings," it is killings that are really on the most -- I'm sorry, at the least, three or four people in one incident. They do not include, for obvious reasons - because otherwise we would go on for page after page after page - the many instances of single killings which took place when villages were taken over by the Serb forces. The Prosecution do not suggest that either accused personally took part in any of these killings, in other words, that they were holding the gun or whatever the implement was that caused death. But we do allege that they bear responsibility for these killings, in that they were a direct result of the policies that they were pursuing in the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And additionally, in the case of Talic, where the perpetrators were known to be members of the forces under his control, he took few, if any, steps to bring them to justice. It has been a matter raised on a number of occasions by counsel for Talic during the pre-trial proceedings that we do not name the perpetrators of the actual killings. In many cases, the majority, we would say, the identity of the actual killers is not known. People who survived the killings or witnessed the killings are only able to say that the people who committed them were Serb soldiers. And that, of course, covers a number of possibilities: that they were members of the regular VRS, or that they were people, reservists, in the territorial units who had been called up, or that they were nothing more than local Serbs who had put on uniform. Nothing in the ARK area reached the scale, in terms of numbers, that the massacre that the world now knows about which took place in Srebrenica, that the numbers were nothing like that. But across the board, there were killings of substantial numbers of men in single incidents, which we suggest show a pattern again. In Kljuc, on or about the 1st of June of 1992, about 100 men were ordered together in the village of Velagici. They were taken to the local school by Serb soldiers. Three men were immediately killed in the front of the school. The remainder were then ordered to leave the building. There was then indiscriminate fire, and nearly all of them were killed. In the same municipality, on the 10th of July - so just over a month later - Serb soldiers -- and on this occasion, there is no doubt who they were. They were members of one of the territorial units which had been brought under Talic's command and were the 17th Light Infantry Brigade. They collected a number of men from a village called Biljani. Again, they were taken to the school. That is a theme that runs across. It was nearly always the school. It may be because simply that was the largest building available. The man in charge of the unit is also known by name, a man named Marko Samardzija. He was recognised by some of the people who actually survived or saw the massacre. At the school, some of those men again were shot in front of the school. Some of them were shot in buildings -- outside buildings near the school. The remainder were taken away in buses and killed elsewhere. Some men were arrested. It was a notorious event. And an investigation was carried out. But the records show that nothing ever happened to those men. They were simply returned to their units. As to the commander, he resigned. He is still alive and well and, as far as we know, walking the streets today. In Prijedor, on the 24th of July of 1992, the infamous Room 3 massacre, with which I have already dealt, took place. On the 25th - so a day later - some 90 men who had been kept in the Ljubija football stadium, as a detention camp, were taken to a nearby iron ore pit. They were being guarded by ten or so Serb soldiers. At the pit, they were taken off in groups of three and executed. Dead and dying men were thrown into the pit. I will deal with exhumations in a little while, but very recently, as Your Honours may have heard, there has been an exhumation taking place at that site. On the 21st of August, 1992, some 200 non-Serbs - because they were mixed on this occasion - were in a convoy being taken to Travnik. They were in two buses, packed into two buses. Their escort was made up of Serb police. The buses were stopped. The men were taken off. And they were murdered. It is what is now known as the Mount Vlasic massacre. Very few of those 200 or so men survived. But Your Honours will be hearing from at least one of those survivors. In Kotor Varos, in November 1992 - as I told Your Honours, the events in Kotor Varos started later than elsewhere in the region - men who had been resisting the Serb attack in the town of Velagici decided to flee. They split into two groups. One group decided to go to Travnik. The group consisted of men, women, and children. This group was captured by members of the VRS. They were taken to a school at Grbavica. There were something like 167 men. The women and children were separated. They were taken off in buses. And Your Honour will hear from one of the then-children or young boys, now an adult, of the gauntlet that they were forced to run before they were able to get on the buses or lorries that had been provided. Those men who were left in the school have never been seen again. And although no bodies have been recovered, the Prosecution suggest that the circumstances are such that they can have only been killed that day. Your Honours, that is a brief description of some of the major killings that took place in this area, but there were, as we say, numerous other, smaller - if that's the right word - killings, leaving aside those that were killed in the attacks. Can I just deal with some of these so-called smaller killing incidents? For example, in Sanski Most, on the 31st of May of 1992, the Serb army attacked the predominantly Muslim village of Vrhpolje. Again, women and children were separated from the men. The men were taken to the Vrhpolje bridge. Killings occurred on the way to the bridge and at the bridge itself. On the same day, men from another village, called Hrustovo, were sheltering in a garage. There were approximately 20 of them. All of those men were killed. In Kljuc, again, on the 1st of June, the village of Prhovo was attacked. Serb soldiers separated the men from the women and children, and the men were taken towards a village called Peci. On the way to that village, on the road, about 20 men were killed. That type of pattern, particularly killings on the bridge or people being forced to jump from the bridge into the water, was repeated over and over again across the municipalities. Was anyone ever prosecuted? Persons in military uniform, whether paramilitary, territorial or professional members of the VRS, came within the jurisdiction of the military court in Banja Luka, not the civilian courts. And what was General Talic's attitude towards prosecution? There were a great many serious crimes committed against the non-Serb population by soldiers under the command of General Talic. Aside from the killings, there were also instances of rape, robbery and theft. Unfortunately, in virtually all cases, the perpetrators of these crimes were not brought to justice. There was a military prosecutor's office attached to the 1st Krajina Corps, and some cases of serious crimes committed by Serb soldiers against the non-Serb population were referred for prosecution. It was basically those that achieved a notoriety which it was impossible to ignore. But in practice, few, if any, Serb perpetrators were actually convicted, let alone punished, for the crimes committed against non-Serbs. Even in cases of mass murder, as in the ones I've just described, Serb soldiers were routinely released back to their units following arrest, and never faced trial or punishment. The commanders of the 1st Krajina Corps would intervene in the judicial process to make sure that their men were not punished. I have dealt with the case of the massacre at Biljani. In respect of the Velagici killings, there the soldiers who were prosecuted and convicted were simply -- the convictions were quashed and the defendants given their freedom with no consequences for their actions. And these miscarriages of justice often occurred in the face of overwhelming evidence of guilt that was available to the prosecution and court. Some of these cases are technically still open today. In contrast to this, Serb soldiers who murdered other Serbs were subject to aggressive and efficient prosecution, and that typically resulted in significant periods of imprisonment for the offenders. The crimes which I suppose could be said to affect good military discipline, such as desertion or armed rebellion or illegal possession of weapons, those were -- desertion really, as far as the Serb soldiers were concerned, they were prosecuted properly. And many of the non-Serb population were themselves prosecuted for possession of the illegal weapons after the orders had been issued or other crimes. They themselves were efficiently prosecuted and convicted. And so we say, Your Honours, the only reasonable conclusion to be drawn, as I said earlier on, particularly in relation to General Talic, is that there was no serious effort or will to prosecute soldiers for crimes they had committed against non-Serbs. Your Honours, may I deal briefly now with exhumations? There, I hope, should be, coming up on Your Honour's screen, a map just showing -- one doesn't need to look at the places -- I think it's maybe because the document is still on the ELMO. That's what's occupying my screen. Yes. Do Your Honours have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in due course -- this obviously doesn't -- the colouring makes it very difficult to scan properly, but it's just to give a general idea of the number of sites. Your Honour, some idea of the extent of the killing of civilians which occurred in the ARK area during the indictment period can be gained by examining the evidence of bodies exhumed since the end of the conflict, and also certificates of death which have been issued by the Bosnian courts. In due course, Your Honours will be hearing evidence from a judge who has dealt with quite a lot of this. The system appears to be that it is possible for a family member to go to court to obtain a declaration of death after a period of time, which, by my recollection, is five years and not seven, which it is in a number of jurisdictions, and Your Honours will hear about the procedures that are followed. The exhumations, as I say, are still, in fact, continuing. There was one very recently at the Ljubija pit area. In the 16 municipalities, some 2.364 bodies have been exhumed from 462 mass and individual graves. Of those 2.000 persons exhumed, about half of them, around just over 1.022, are known to have disappeared in 1992. Of the remainder, some 3.6 per cent disappeared between 1993 and 1995, so after the period of the indictment, but for the remainder of the exhumed remains, no year of death can be determined. Now, of the 31 killings which we have listed in paragraph 38 of the indictment, 452 persons coming from 20 of the incidents, have been exhumed and identified. Of the killings set out in paragraph 41, which is the killings that occurred in detention facilities, 240 remains have been exhumed relating to 4 of the actual killings. Court records have been received from eight municipalities producing certificates of death. They relate to some 1.589 individuals who have been missing since 1992 but for whom no bodies have ever been recovered. Your Honours, I have very nearly concluded what I have to say. Before I return to effectively summarise the overall picture that we say represents the two accused's activities, can I just very briefly explain the structure by which we will call the evidence. As Your Honours know, for the sake of coherence, the evidence will be called on a municipality-by-municipality basis, roughly we hope in a chronological order of the events. It can to a certain extent create an uneven picture because, as we say, the -- one of the telling facts in this case is the pattern that emerges. But we hope at the end of that evidence to be able to present that to Your Honours in some kind of diagrammatic schedule form. Obviously, we will have to wait until the evidence has been heard. I have looked in this opening at the thematic elements of the evidence because this is not a case where the accused are the actual physical perpetrators of the crimes. Their responsibility arises from their roles in the planning, the instigation, the ordering, the execution of this campaign that we say existed to permanently remove non-Serbs by the condition of the crimes alleged in this indictment. The case will start with evidence from the municipality of Banja Luka, because it was the base for the ARK Crisis Staff, it was where the headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps were located. As I've already referred to that municipality, it is perhaps the exception to the rule. The pattern that is discernible across the other municipalities during the course of 1992 is not seen so strongly in Banja Luka. Many of the lesser persecutory elements are present: the denial of rights, the removal of non-Serbs from their work, the removal from their residences, and the like. And certainly there were police forces or paramilitary forces, in particular -- Your Honours will hear about what is described as the red kombi, a red van, which went round the streets of Banja Luka, pulling in people of non-Serb ethnicity, beating them, and taking them to the police station where further beatings took place. But it never reached the heights in Banja Luka in 1992 of any of the other municipalities. There may be many reasons for this: It was too visible for the crude, not to say brutal, techniques which were applied in many other municipalities; it had constant visits from members of the International Community -- David Owen, as he then was, Lord Owen, and Mr. Vance went there when they were negotiating -- relief organisations providing humanitarian aid or aid to refugees operated from there. Accordingly, many of the witnesses who come from the ethnic -- from the non-Serb ethnic make-up did survive 1992, without perhaps more than harassment or some kind of occasionally beatings. But they were allowed to survive and remain during 1992. One of the aspects that Your Honours may think emerges from the evidence that -- what was actually taking place was a gradual encirclement of Banja Luka, as one municipality after another came under complete Serb control. What about the witnesses themselves? Many of them will be giving evidence of crimes which were perpetrated upon them or upon family members or crimes to which they were witnesses, crimes of an egregious nature. Others will give evidence of the political aspects of what happened, more of an overview. It is worth remembering that all of them are describing now events which happened ten years ago. And I don't think one needs to have an expert to come and tell us that memories fade after ten years. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In addition, the Prosecution will call persons with expertise in fields which are relevant to this indictment where they have conducted analyses of the evidence. For example, there will be expertise or expert evidence called about command and control issues which arise in relation to the military; about religious destruction; demographers - and as Your Honours know, the first witness will be the historian, Dr. Donia - and constitutional experts, very briefly, just to give the expert view on the crisis staff and to explain some of the terminology that does come up over and over again in the documents and from the witnesses in this case. And of course, apart from the testimony of witnesses, the Prosecution rely on documentary evidence which was either seized by way of a search warrant some years ago now in the area or provided by witnesses or other organisations. Your Honours, finally, can I come back, then, to what is of course the issue in this case, the responsibility of the accused. This has been set out in the pre-trial brief in relation to each accused in respect of each municipality. What I propose now is simply to summarise that. The Prosecution say that both of the two accused were in positions of responsibility. Both were close to the persons who, first of all, through the medium of the political party, the SDS, and then when the SDS became the government, which was established in the areas now known as Republika Srpska, they were the main public figures in this enterprise to create the Serbian state. Radoslav Brdjanin, from September of 1992, was directly involved in that government as a minister. General Talic, as Commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, reported directly to the main staff of the VRS and effectively to its chief, General Mladic. Certain of the persons to whom these two accused were close and closely linked have been indicted and so are specifically named in this indictment - that is to say Radovan Karadzic, not yet arrested, Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic - but of course there were others not indicted and not named. The Prosecution in this case does not have to prove the guilt of any of the others named. They are not charged in this indictment. The Prosecution, we submit, has to prove that there was a criminal enterprise and that these two accused knowingly and wilfully joined that enterprise and within that enterprise played the roles that their positions assigned them to. As far as Radoslav Brdjanin is concerned, the Prosecution say that from early 1991, and in particular from the time that the Association of Bosnian Krajina Municipalities was formed, from that time, he was a leading figure, not only in the politics of the Krajina but on a wider front through his activities as an SDS deputy to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is before the creation of the Serbian Assembly. But he was one of the founding members of that Assembly of the Serbian People. Intercepted telephone communications show direct contact with Radovan Karadzic in the lead up to the cataclysmic events of 1992. On the 12th of July of 1991, the SDS held a meeting in Sarajevo. Brdjanin attended as a delegate from the Bosnian Krajina, together in fact with Vojo Kupresanin. And during the discussions or speeches, he set out what the Prosecution suggest was his personal creed: "I am a man who abides by two principles. I obey and respect those who are above me. All those who are under my command must obey me." We suggest these are not the words of a man who was, or would be prepared to be, no more than a figurehead, a puppet. His words and actions demonstrate not only a man committed to the creation of a Serbian state but a man ready to use, and encourage others to use, unlawful methods, violence, to achieve that goal. In June or July of 1992, whilst so-called combat operations were under way in Kotor Varos, being undertaken in fact by units of the 1st Krajina Corps, Brdjanin visited the area and he was interviewed on television. Your Honours, I'm going to ask that be played but we have for Your Honours a transcript, an English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this the paper which was handed out yesterday by any chance?

utterances.text: It is, if Your Honours have that. And I think Defence counsel have been given a copy. If that video clip --

utterances.text: Can we have four photocopies -- or seven photocopies made before you proceed, Ms. Korner?

utterances.text: Certainly. I do apologise.

utterances.text: I realise this was circulated yesterday, and between then and today, it will not be the first time it may have been mislaid, but I would like you to proceed only when the Defence team have it in front of them, and it's only going to take one minute maximum to ... Do you require more copies? This is why I said seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I don't think co-counsel can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.text: I think you can go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. If we could just play the video clip, then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "REPORTER: Tell us, Mr. Brdjanin, about the reasons of your arrival and how would you assess the most recent events in the region of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRDJANIN
utterances.text: It was my duty as the President of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region to visit all the theatres of war. However, I must admit that I was visiting the corridor most of all of the time. But the reason for my arrival is that every Monday I have to report to all the presidents of the Crisis Staff on the political situation in this region. We have to sweep through our region, that is through Kotor Varos and Jajce, and the most important ongoing battle I saw yesterday is the battle for penetration towards Serbia. We realise that negotiations with the enemy side have become impossible, for those who have taken up weapons must be defeated. They have to hand in their weapons and total Serbian authority must be imposed here."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, it would appear that the person Your Honours saw briefly at the beginning of the clip firing -- or on a tank was in fact, as the translation suggests, Radoslav Brdjanin. Your Honour, the importance, we say, is what he's actually saying. And it encapsulates his attitude and really the role of the crisis staff. "It is my duty as the president of the crisis staff of the Autonomous Region to visit all of the theatres of war; however, I must admit that I was visiting the corridor most of the time. But the reason for my arrival is that every Monday, I have to report to all the presidents of the crisis staffs on the political situation in this region. We have to sweep through our region, that is, through Kotor Varos and Jajce, and the most important ongoing battle I saw yesterday is the battle for penetration towards Serbia. We realise that the negotiations with the enemy side have become impossible, for those who have taken up weapons must be defeated. They have to hand in their weapons, and total Serbian authority must be imposed here." Your Honours, it may be as well to remind ourselves that the municipality of Kotor Varos had a 38 per cent population that declared itself Serbian, 30 per cent Muslim, and 29 per cent Croatian. The Prosecution say that Radoslav Brdjanin was rightly regarded as an extremist and that in the positions that he occupied, particularly as president of the ARK Crisis Staff, he was at the very least - and we say it went a great deal further than that - able to influence the decisions and the actions taken at the municipality level at which the -- at which level the crimes were being committed. Your Honours will hear evidence about the actual involvement of members of those crisis staffs in the commission of crimes, in particular in places such as Sanski Most and Kljuc. We say those people who actually took part in the actual crimes were doing so with the full knowledge and indeed with the -- if one can put it this way, at the instigation of the president of the regional crisis staff. Your Honour, with respect to General Talic, to sum up his role -- I spent some time yesterday dealing with his role, but what one can say is this: The 1st Krajina Corps was the largest and most experienced corps of the Bosnia Serb army, the VRS. From its establishment, it undertook a mobilisation and expansion process that continued during the summer of 1992. It took control of all the Serb Territorial Defence units and other armed formations that were not already operating as units of the corps. The VRS was organised around a comprehensive military document -- doctrine - I'm sorry - and a series of laws. The application of those doctrines and laws was codified in the rules and regulations which governed all levels and organs of the military. General Talic had been in the JNA, as it was, the VRS, as it became, for over 30 years by the time of these events and we suggest was well suited and well understood the obligations that his role as commander of this corps imposed upon him. If one looks briefly at just a few of the municipalities in which his corps operated, just to remind ourselves of what was happening there. From the documents, from his own corps documents, it becomes plain. But for example, in Prijedor, he commandered the military operations against the Muslim armed groups and the Muslim population, in particular, in Hambarine and Kozarac. We say from those documents he knew at this time that soldiers under his command were taking revenge on the civilian population in Prijedor. When Hambarine, a predominantly Muslim village, was attacked by his forces, civilian housing and the civilian population became the target of the attack. General Talic knew that units under his command had "sealed" the town of Kozarac that Your Honours saw in that brief video clip. He reported that 80 to 100 Muslim men were killed and 1.500 had been captured. It would appear that the numbers killed were considerably higher. And Your Honours will be hearing evidence to the effect that he was told that these numbers were higher but reduced the numbers when reporting it to his superiors. And from the end of May into June, both members of the VRS and the Serb police forces continued to disarm, to capture, and to liquidate members of the non-Serb population. In fact, General Talic reported to his superiors that something like 7.000 Muslims from the Prijedor area had been detained in the Omarska and Trnopolje camps. Security around the Trnopolje camp was provided by units who came under Talic's command. And I don't need to remind Your Honours again of his connection with the Manjaca prison camp. As far as Sanski Most is concerned, by the end of April of 1992, all the key installations in Sanski Most had come under the control of the 6th Partisan Brigade, the Serbian Territorial Brigade, and the police. In May, he reported that forces under his command were controlling Sanski Most. Serb forces, the VRS, shelled the predominantly Muslim villages of Hrustovo, a Muslim area in Sanski Most; Mahala; and the Muslim village of Vrhpolje. There was large-scale looting and plunder of Muslim and Croat property carried out by members of his units. Units under his command were engaged, we suggest, in the destruction of housing and religious buildings that were in the Sanski Most area. And throughout May and June, there were many arrests of Muslim and Croat men in Sanski Most. Those arrested were interrogated, and many of them, if not most, were severely beaten. It was units under his command that were responsible for bringing in nearly all these people to the Sanski Most Detention Centres. Again, they provided security at those centres. And the crisis staff in Sanski Most resolved - they actually drafted a resolution which we have a copy of - to send the prisoners who were politicians, nationalist extremists, or unwelcome in Sanski Most to the VRS camp in Manjaca. That had to be arranged through Talic's command. And throughout the period, he reported on what is described as "mopping up and disarming" through June of 1992. Celinac, which we haven't really dealt with, because it was a municipality with an overwhelming Serb majority. And by and large in those municipalities, the events of 1992 were not so dramatic or so devastating. But even there - and came within Talic's area of responsibility - he was aware that in August of 1992 attacks had taken place on villages called Velagici and Samac. And he was aware that civilians had been killed and that houses belonging to Muslims had been destroyed. And in August he was aware that a light infantry brigade under his command, was, as he put it, taking its revenge - those are the words of the English translation of the words that were used - on the Muslim population around Celinac, and he knew that this type of conduct was becoming exceedingly frequent. Your Honours, I could go on but Your Honours have seen it in the pre-trial brief. I've just selected three municipalities as an example. Your Honours, in respect of General Talic, we say that he was ideologically committed to this cause. He was not just a military officer obeying orders. We say that he shared the intention of his co-accused, Radoslav Brdjanin, to, as it were, expel from the areas that were regarded as properly belonging to the Serbian state that was to be created by the use of unlawful criminal methods. And, Your Honour, we say that becomes apparent from his own documents, what was said and everything that we know about General Talic. At the end of the day, as I said when I started this opening yesterday, it is Your Honours who decide on what is the proper evidence in this case, what the evidence shows, and whether the Crown -- whether the Prosecution proved its case. Your Honour, we say at the end of the evidence, Your Honours can be satisfied so that you are sure that the Prosecution has proved its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one very brief objection that I would like to lodge that I did not want to interrupt her for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner seems to be taking the position that Mr. Brdjanin was at the very least a person of influence, a man of influence, who could have influenced certain events. I want to object to any suggestion by Ms. Korner that that has legal significance. That issue was raised by the Prosecution, argued vigorously and decided against them by the Appeals Chamber in the Celebici case. They were alleging that one of the persons in that case should have been convicted because he was a person of influence and could have influenced persons over whom he did not have a superior relationship - they were not his subordinates - just because of his influence, and that was soundly rejected, and that decision is binding not just on the Prosecutor and me but all of us, including the Trial Chambers. To the extent she is suggesting that is the law, it's not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner? If you want to rebut this, you can, and please try, in as short a time as possible, also to touch upon the other two matters that you wanted to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have set out the legal modes of liability, and I thought I had made it clear we do not suggest that it's influence. We suggest it is instigation, ordering and all the other modes of liability that we have set out. If I used -- if it was taken that I was suggesting that mere influence was sufficient to found a conviction, then I'm sorry, it was never intended so to do. Clearly, the modes of -- by which these offences can be committed are set out. Your Honour, very briefly, then, two matters that I wish to raise. Firstly this: When Your Honours -- when Your Honour yesterday was talking about treating a witness as a hostile witness, in, I think, Your Honour's jurisdiction and my jurisdiction, that arises when a witness, who is expected to give evidence in accordance with the statement they've made, suddenly departs from it and shows an attitude which is hostile to the person calling them. And it is, I think in our jurisdictions, you cannot call a witness that you know doesn't wish to give evidence and will not give evidence in that effect. Now, it's different, I know, in the United States, where the person calling a witness is allowed to call a witness whom he knows is hostile but then allowed to treat him as a hostile witness virtually ab initio. I was unaware that there was any provision really in this Tribunal whereby one could deal with that, but if there is, it might assist if Your Honour were to make it clear which kind of system --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the system that this Trial Chamber opts for is that if you bring forward a witness, you are expected not to attack the credibility of that witness. In other words, we are talking of your witness. And therefore, you are expected to bring forward witnesses that you have consulted with beforehand, that more or less you know what kind of evidence they are going to produce. Now, if that witness, at any point in time in the course of the testimony, turns against you and disrupts what you had planned to get from that particular witness, him or her being your witness, then obviously you are going to be faced with a difficult situation and it may well be that you would prefer to bring forward previous statements made by that witness that are contradictory to what that witness would be stating during these proceedings. This is what I am referring to. You will not be allowed to contradict the witness until you first obtain the permission of the Trial Chamber to do so. In other words, once you have taken the decision to produce that witness as your witness in support of your case, then the practice ought to be that you do not try to discredit your own witness. But if you need to discredit your own witness at any point in time, obviously, you will be allowed to do that provided the Tribunal, the Chamber, is satisfied that that witness has turned hostile.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That is very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the position. Have I made it also clear -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must say I am not familiar with the Anglo-Saxon method. What does this mean to discredit the witness? To contradict him in order to discredit him? Or is it necessary to attack his honour and his integrity? I'm a bit lost in these concepts which are quite alien to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are not as alien as you think, Mr. de Roux. It can happen to the Prosecution; it can happen to the Defence. There may come a time when you produce a witness and -- thinking that that witness is going to state certain facts which would go in favour of your client, and in actual fact, to your surprise, that witness all of a sudden becomes a hostile witness, that witness will say exactly the opposite, or that witness will refuse to answer questions to which you know, and your client knows, he or she has got a very straightforward answer. You may need at that point in time to justify the fact that you have brought forward that witness, because no one expects you, as a competent Defence lawyer, to bring forward witnesses that will harm rather than help the cause of your client. So the rule is that once you have chosen to bring forward a witness, it's because you believe in the credibility of that witness. Otherwise, as I pointed out to you yesterday, you have a duty not to bring forward witnesses that are not going to say the truth. That is a duty which each counsel has. If you, in other words, produce a witness, it's because you know, you're confident, that he or she is going to tell the truth and that truth is going to go in favour of your client, or at least benefit the course of justice, the search for truth. If that doesn't happen, you are in a difficulty, and it may well be that you will need to discredit your own witness, in other words to say that that -- to prove to the Court or show to the Court that that witness is telling a lie now because he is used to telling lies, that that witness is telling a lie now because you have ample evidence that on previous occasions, he had stated this and that, which is exactly the opposite of what he or she is stating now, and that would justify also your decision to bring forward that witness to testify in front of this Tribunal in favour of your client. Otherwise, it doesn't make sense. So this is not actually -- it is given more emphasis and more importance in Anglo-Saxon and common-law practices, but it is also a problem that has arisen before this Tribunal in other cases, and on which there has been more or less a practice that has been adopted. In other words, you will be, as such, entitled to treat that witness as a hostile witness and also try to discredit that witness and also bring forward prior, contradictory statements only if you first seek the permission of the Tribunal, and the Tribunal will give that permission if that -- if there is relevance to the evidence that you would like to bring forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand fully, Mr. President. After all, all systems resemble one another eventually. It's just a manner of expressing ourselves that differ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I obviously used a term which is more -- more or less belongs and is used more in common law jurisdictions. You know, I mean -- but I hope I have made myself understood. I mean, it will not create big problems. More or less it's a rule that follows -- it's a consequence to the rule that you should not bring forward witnesses that you know are not going to say the truth. And as a consequence, him or her being your witness, I have to -- you have to cover yourself and you have to cover also the whole proceedings. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only other matter I want to raise -- and perhaps I know it's time to the break. If I can just bring it to Your Honour's attention. Your Honour did not deal with the Rule which is 90(H)(ii). And I think Your Honour perhaps ought to deal with it because it's not a rule that is familiar, as I understand it, to the civil systems. And indeed, I think even in the United States it's not an obligation to put your case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But Ms. Korner, I think the life of this Tribunal risks -- already has an inherent risk in matters of cross-examination, not because counsel like you coming from jurisdictions where cross-examination is part of advocacy and is an art in itself but because we have other lawyers here, other counsel, coming from a jurisdiction where cross-examination as such is not institutionalised. And this is perhaps one reason why this paragraph is included in the Rules. I think I do not need to explain it. I would suppose that Mr. de Roux and Mr. Pitron are fully aware of it, and I would suppose that Mr. Ackerman also is aware of it, although, as you say, it is not quite akin to the -- or does not form part of the jurisdictions around the various states in the US. It's one Rule that has to be observed. But I don't need to explain it. I mean, all I need to explain is that you're not expected to make a whole speech to the witness before you start your cross-examination, and a witness may have given evidence on a particular event, and you are to address the cross-examination on what actually has been stated by the witness in examination-in-chief. That is the main rule of the cross-examination. Anyway, the Rules are there. You have (H)(i), and (H)(ii), and (H)(iii), and more or less you are expected to follow those Rules. What I can tell you is that I will not allow across -- an across-the-board cross-examination dealing with cabbages and kings. I mean, the Rules have to be observed. If paragraph 1 says that "Cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the evidence in chief and matters affecting the credibility of the witness and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party to the subject matter of that case," that's what the cross-examination has to be limited to. Then obviously there may be instances where we have to open a little bit or restrict a little bit. But again, I think we will have to play it by the ear. I don't know as yet how it's going to go. I still have to wait and see what kind of cross-examinations we will have. And I will direct -- conduct the orchestra as we go along. But I would imagine that -- I'm not going to explain to experienced lawyers coming from -- from --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't asking Your Honour to explain it. I was simply asking Your Honour to draw the attention to -- of counsel to this. And Mr. Ackerman I know has practiced here for a number of years. But it has -- it is a problem that has arisen in other cases because it is not a feature of the civil law system to say to a witness when your case is -- "I suggest to you," or however you put it, "that what you are saying is not the truth," or "you are mistaken," or however you wish to put it. And so witnesses go away without that feature ever having been put and then have to be brought back at vast expense, extending the trial, if it's important enough, for that matter to be dealt with. And that's the only reason I'm raising it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, we will break now until 11.00. And I understand we will resume with the evidence of Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour -- I'm sorry, may I just say Mr. Ackerman gave me a document this morning which he is going to ask Dr. Donia about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want two days?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I want two days, yes -- no, I just wanted an opportunity -- I don't know if Dr. Donia has been brought down here yet, but I wanted him to have an opportunity to look at that document before he's called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So are you suggesting that we start a little bit later than 11.00?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Could Your Honours say five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start at five past -- or let me have -- please send me a message whether five past 11.00 is okay or whether you prefer ten past. It depends. In the meantime, may I confirm -- have a confirmation from Mr. Ackerman and Mr. de Roux that you are not going to make your opening statements. That's the indication you gave last Friday or last Monday. So do you confirm it, that you are not going to make your opening statement now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I confirm that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm that also, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Brdjanin, and General Talic, I put the same question to you last time. utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.text: All right. So we will break until ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we proceed with the evidence of the first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we can. There was just a preliminary matter - actually a number of preliminary matters - which hopefully will not give rise to any kind of dispute between the parties but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I hope, I hope. The numbering of exhibits. You had alluded to the matter yesterday during -- I think just before Ms. Korner's opening, and you had stated that we would use P for Prosecution exhibits and D for Defence exhibits, but in terms of the numbering system, I've had a short conversation about this with Mr. Ackerman - I have not spoken to my French colleagues - but if we are to use the disclosure numbers of the Prosecutor, we are going to find that the order in which the exhibits proceed in the case will obviously not be sequential - you will have P7.221, P1.4, P1.5 - because obviously the order of calling exhibits is not going to be the same as the order in which they were disclosed. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I personally do not have an objection provided, number 1, that a proper record is kept of how this goes along; secondly, that it does not cause too much trouble and problems and work for the Deputy Registrar, and that, in other words, it's something that they can cope with; and thirdly, I would also like to hear the Defence first on whether they have any particular objection. If that is okay, if it's okay with the staff to go along, I mean, I have -- and I would understand that my colleagues here don't -- you don't have an objection about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can go ahead. We don't foresee this causing you any undue problems.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In the Registry, we are very flexible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So you can do it that way, yes. The Chamber doesn't have any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In respect of Dr. Donia, just before he comes in, what I have done to assist my colleagues opposite is to have our staff prepare a binder of the documents which he will be referring to in his evidence. All of those documents are referred to in the footnotes of his report. One of the documents has not been disclosed to the Defence. I've already informed Mr. Pitron and Mr. Ackerman about that.
