utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me clarify myself on that. I have read the -- Dr. Donia's report in its entirety. The first 23, 24 pages, frankly, I mean, there is a lot of material which was interesting to know and interesting to read, but to be frank with you, I don't know how relevant it is for the purpose of -- purposes of this trial. Then there are a couple of pages especially when he deals with certain cultural and religious aspects, that may be important to know. It also gives his own personal view on the matter and also passes judgement on the judgement passed by other people on what actually caused whatever happened in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia where you may encounter problems in the course of his evidence. I think for the present moment, I would invite you to conduct your examination-in-chief of Mr. Donia in a sense as to restrict it as much as possible as to what is really relevant for the purposes of this trial. This trial covers, first of all, the jurisdiction of this Tribunal is limited to a certain -- to certain events that happened in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia in a particular period, and this trial then is further limited. So I leave it up to you for the moment. I mean, use your good judgement. Maybe I will have to stop you in due course if I think that you are moving out of what I think ought to be the parameters of the evidence of Dr. Donia. But please feel free to conduct your examination-in-chief without the fear of being interrupted repeatedly and repeatedly and repeatedly. I will leave you as much freedom as you wish. But then, of course, there may be limitations to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And this map -- I know yesterday you were saying that the map was too small, so we've got a slightly larger map. I don't intend to offer it into evidence, but the witness will be referring to it briefly during the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I see on the monitor how that map would appear, because it's not in a position which can be seen by the Defence counsel, and I want -- Can you see it from there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can see it from there. Okay. So okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can call the witness, with your permission, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Call Dr. Donia in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you solemnly declare to say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, could you spell your name for the transcript, please, your full name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's Robert J. -- middle name is J-a-y, last name is Donia, D-o-n-i-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you're an American citizen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if you could very briefly give to the Judges a summary of your academic qualifications and positions that you have held and a summary of your publications, both books and articles that you have written in connection with your particular expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first became involved in the history of the former Yugoslavia in 1972 when I began a Ph.D. programme in history at the University of Michigan. I spent the academic year 1974/1975 in Sarajevo doing research in preparation for a doctoral dissertation, and completed that dissertation in 1976. That work with revisions became a book in 1981 published under the title "Islam Under the Double Eagle: The Muslims of Bosnia and Hercegovina, 1878 to 1914." After completing the doctoral dissertation, I taught for two years at the Ohio State University Lima Campus as an assistant professor, for one year at the University of Oregon, and at that point left the academic work completely and spent the next 18 years employed by the securities firm of Merrill Lynch. During that time, I had no relationship with the former Yugoslavia, except that in 1994 Professor John Fine and I together wrote a book which was a survey history of Bosnia and Herzegovina called "Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Tradition Betrayed." I retired from Merrill Lynch in 1998, and since then have been working on a study of the city -- history of the city of Sarajevo since 1878.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've published a number of articles very recently in connection with your interest in Yugoslavia. What current academic positions do you hold at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I currently have two affiliations. I am affiliated with the Centre for Russian and East European Studies at the University of Michigan, and I'm a visiting scholar at the Department of History of the University of California at San Diego.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the last ten years, how much time have you spent in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until my retirement, I probably was somewhere in the former Yugoslavia only about three weeks a year. Since then, it's perhaps been about three months a year, in the last, say, three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've testified before the Tribunal before. Can you tell the Judges which cases you've appeared in as an expert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified in the Prosecutor v. Tihomir Blaskic and prepared a presentation or paper and testified in the case of the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez. I submitted a written -- I made a written submission in the case of the Prosecutor v. Miroslav Kvocka, the Omarska case. And I testified and prepared a written presentation in the case of the people -- or the Prosecutor v. Blagoje Simic, the Bosanski Samac case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you have any personal or ethical problems which would preclude you from testifying in any particular case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you consider testifying for the Defence in any particular case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would consider any invitation to work with -- with the Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the report that we asked you to produce in this case, can you explain to the Judges exactly what we requested from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor requested from me a background report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me interrupt you. Was this request a written document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you specify your needs and your request by means of a letter, by means of a written document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. The report was essentially the product of discussion between staff in the OTP and Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Because if it was the result of a written document, then obviously I would ask you to bring it forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In discussions, the Office of the Prosecutor asked me to prepare a report on the historical background to events alleged in the indictment, to include the pre-history of the period and also the immediate political and social developments in the period from 1990 until about the middle of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I know in our discussions, there are a number of typographical corrections which I think we should do now, and there are some factual corrections that we should also put in, so if you could -- I can direct you to the pages and you can explain to the Court the corrections that need to be made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I apologise for these -- there are a number of typographical errors. A few of them have substance or are the result of an actual error in information, and I'd like to at least correct the latter, starting on page 44, the fourth line. I believe his name is Dr. Dusko Jaksic, not Drago. Apologies to him as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fourth line on page 44, Mr. President. On that same page, the -- after the indented quote, on the fourth line of the next paragraph, it says, "On April 10, 1992." That should be, "April 10, 1991." And also on that page, in the next paragraph, the fifth line, there is a sentence that begins, "The nine members." That should be, "Most members." On page 45, after the first indented quote, "SDS spokesmen" should be "SDP spokesmen." On page 48, the title for table 2 should be "Nationality in Municipalities Invited to Join Bosnian Krajina" instead of "That Joined." On page 55 is another error of date. In the first full paragraph of the section, The Arms Buildup, right after footnote 167, "On June 10, 1992" should be, "June 10, 1991." And finally, on page 67, the first full paragraph, second line, "Agreement reached in Brussels" should read "Lisbon." And on page -- there is the same error on page 66, where it reads "Brussels" and it should read "Lisbon."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I got lost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On page 57, it is in the first paragraph, full paragraph, starting with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 67, yes, second line, "Brussels" should be substituted with "Lisbon."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't find "Brussels" on page 66.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 66, "Brussels" is at the fourth-to-last line on the page. I said it correctly the first two times and then changed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. "Lisbon" as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's all I can find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're a good professor, very few mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, your report is essentially structured into four parts, and if you could just very briefly explain to the judges what those four parts are?

The first part of the report is a brief snapshot of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia in 1990-1991, just before the outbreak of armed conflict. The second section is a brief discussion of a widely-held misunderstanding of the history of the region, known as the ancient-tribal-hatreds myth. The third section, which starts on page 5, is a historical survey from the migration of the South Slavs up to 1990. And the fourth section of the paper is the developments after 1990, 1990 and after, in other words after the fall of communism and the developments in that decade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can turn to the first page of your report, Part I, and in your written report, you essentially identify two events which you state lead to war in the former Yugoslavia, and I wonder, could you explain that to the judges, exactly what you set out there, just summarise what you said?

Well, I'd say they preceded war. The first was the collapse of the Yugoslav League of Communists in January, 1990. The second was the elections, multi-party elections, that occurred in each republic of the former Yugoslavia in the course of 1990. And the third significant development for understanding the situation was the completion of the decennial census in the spring of 1991, which gives us the best profile of the population composition of the republics of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Yugoslavia in 1990, and what -- the places that concern this case are Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia and Croatia - principally Bosnia-Herzegovina, less so Serbia and Croatia. Can you give the Judges some sense of the population distribution in those three places, very briefly Serbia and Croatia, and then obviously more fully Bosnia-Herzegovina?

The population in the Republic of Serbia, to the east of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was of course a majority of those of Serbian nationality. In the so-called autonomous region, or the province of Voyvodina, there was a substantial Hungarian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if it would assist the Court, you can briefly refer to this map, if you wish to stand up and use the pointer.

Do I have one? Here, okay. This is -- the Republic of Serbia as it existed in 1990 includes all this area. The area of Voyvodina to the north with the substantial Hungarian population is here, and to the south of course is the area of Kosovo known by many Serbs as -- referred to by many Serbs as Kosovo Metohija and by many Albanians as Kosova. The population in this region is majority Albanian, a little over -- a little under 90 per cent Albanian as of 1991. The Republic of Croatia, since wrapped around the shape of Bosnia, had a majority population of those of the Croatian nationality but it also had a substantial minority of Serbs, about 600.000, a little less, about 12 per cent of the population. Some of those Serbs lived in the cities of Croatia. Others were in the area to the north where there were some villages and areas of Serbian population, and also in this highland area here, in the hinterlands of the Dalmatian coast.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So to be specific for the Court's record, you're stating that there were people of Serbian ethnicity living to the north of the Bosnia-Herzegovina border and to the east of that border?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, to the west of that border?

Yes. And the developments of the late 1980s and 1990 led, in Serbia, to the rise of -- to power of Slobodan Milosevic, first as president of the League of Communists of Serbia and later as the President of Serbia, and in 1990 to the election of Franjo Tudjman as President of Croatia, so that each of these neighbouring republics, the people in power had cultivated an interest in their kin populations within Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina itself was a mixed republic. It was the only one of the six republics of the former Yugoslavia that did not have a single nationality in the majority. And the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You can take a seat now, Dr. Donia. And since you're moving on to the ethnic distribution in Bosnia, do you have map two of your report? If you don't, you can use my copy. It's a composite part of the entire report.
I do not have the maps in front of me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated to the Court that Bosnia-Herzegovina was the only essentially truly mixed population of any -- it was the only republic that had a truly mixed population. I wonder if you could just briefly explain to the Judges how the different ethnic groups were distributed throughout the country.

Most of the country was a population mix of two or, in many cases, three of the nationalities, that is, the Serbs, Croats, and Bosnian Muslims. There were very few areas where one could define a population that was purely of one single nationality. But there are a few worthy of note. The first one is the area in blue to the kind of lower left side of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you point that out.

This area here, which is -- particularly a couple of the municipalities, a virtually 100 per cent Croat area; an area of north-western -- extreme North-Western Bosnia, which is nearly 100 per cent Muslim; and then this border area adjoining Croatia with a population -- it's not a very dense population. It's largely rural territory. But it's virtually 100 per cent Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Cayley. Let me interrupt you for a second. I take it that this map is not one that you prepared yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have borrowed it from the census that was prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the 1991 census. And this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is an official map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not. It's one of many that was prepared by individual companies after the 1991 census. I believe I have a source notation in the appendix. I must say that it's -- it's extremely difficult to capture on any map the ethnic picture of Bosnia. I happen to believe this perhaps does the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is important for us at this juncture to know exactly the exact -- the proper origin of this map. Who prepared it? Just to make sure that this was prepared by someone who had no interest in presenting a map which does not represent the truth or which twists the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's referred to Dr. Donia's map two in Appendix B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But it is obviously not a map prepared by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you want to go to the appendix, you can state on the record --
Yes, it was prepared by a group called Ultramedia in Sarajevo, published in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia, you just indicated that the area in red essentially on the Croatian border was an area that was inhabited predominantly by people of Serbian ethnicity. Are there any other comments you'd like to make about this map or about ethnic distribution in Bosnia-Herzegovina?
There are specific historical reasons why these enclaves developed. But I think we can cover that momentarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you wish to mention that now, or do you wish to mention --
Sure. The northern one-third of this area, roughly this region here, is known as the Bosnian Krajina. And the Bosnian Krajina shared a destiny --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's on, my microphone. Dr. Donia, could you please just repeat what you just stated and indicate the same portion of the territory on the map over there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the benefit of Defence counsel.

The northern one-third, roughly northern one-third of Bosnia-Herzegovina constitutes an area known as the Bosnian Krajina. The term "Krajina" means borderland or boundary area. And this is an area that developed a specific -- has had a specific history within Bosnia-Herzegovina and has in some sense a counterpart region on the other side of the boundary with Croatia. Namely, starting in the seventeenth century, that boundary became the border with Austria, the Austrian Empire, and the Ottoman Empire. And during that time, the authorities of those respective empires, the Ottomans and the Austrians, wanted to fortify these border regions. And to do so, they established incentives for those of Serbian Orthodox religion to migrate to the areas that are in these two Krajinas, the Croatian -- the Krajina on the Croatian side and the Bosnian Krajina. Consequently, there were historically a large number of Serbs that moved into this region. There were also fortifications on the extreme north-western area, starting in the seventeenth century, of castles and fortifications by Muslims, who -- in service of the Ottoman Empire. So that goes quite a ways to explain this enclave of Muslim concentration here and these enclaves or the enclave of Serbian concentration, both here and in some of the borderlands along the northern part. It also, of course, explains the presence of a substantial number of rural Serbs in the Krajina area across the border in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if we can move now to page 5 of your report. And you have a paragraph which is headed "The Myth of Ancient Tribal Hatreds." And if you could explain what you mean to the Judges in respect of those three paragraphs in your report.

Well, this notion that the South Slav peoples have been killing one another for centuries and living in perpetual hatred arose in the early 1990s among western observers as something of a myth of convenience. It enabled them to distance themselves from events in the Balkans. It was welcomed by some nationalists among the South Slavs who wished to portray the history of their own nations as a series of repressive acts or violence undertaken against them. But I find little evidence for this kind of religious or national animosity until the very nineteenth century and twentieth century. For -- over most years, in most times prior to that, the people in the very broad mixture of Bosnia-Herzegovina lived side by side together without substantial armed strife. There was plenty of violence, but it was typically of a social variety or wars concerning the establishment of boundaries, for example, medieval feudal lords fighting over territory and other territorial disputes over the centuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I would suggest to you to restrict this part as much as possible, because we are not interested much in what happened in the last century and in the centuries before. I mean, try to direct your witness to what is relevant to this -- to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Without dedicating much time and effort on the myth of ancient tribal hatreds. I don't think anyone coming from the territory of Yugoslavia needs to receive any lessons on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of the history, there are one or two matters which I believe are relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Come to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- in the indictment, and that's where I'm going now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Come to those, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, in part 3 of your report, you do a historical survey to 1990. And the areas that particularly interest me are page 13 - if you could turn to that page - which is the rise of nationalism. But prior to that, you sort of broadly refer to it. Within the Krajina region, what by 1990 were the three confessional groups, the three ethnicities living in that region?
Well, the three nations were the Bosnian Muslims and the Serbs and then also some Croats. Fewer Croats, but some Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you explain very briefly from a historical perspective why there was a rise in nationalism amongst these groups seeking some form of national identity.

The rise of nationalism is, in fact, the articulation of a political programme that can be dated to the nineteenth century, in the case of Serbs and Croats, and to the twentieth century, in the case of the Bosnian Muslims. And in espousing these political goals and searching for some sort of state structure in which their group would find either autonomy or independence, the Serbs and Croats each developed something of a historical understanding or narrative which emphasised certain events.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain -- and we'll deal with each of the ethnic groups, but can you explain how the Serb national identity began to form in the region.

Well, the Serbian national understanding really focused on a close relationship with the Serbian Orthodox Church, and the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 is particularly important in this understanding. And in folk poetry and broad popular understanding, at that battle, the leader of the Serbs, Prince Lazar, was offered a choice of a heavenly kingdom and an earthly kingdom, and in opting for a heavenly kingdom was promised that an earthly kingdom would be restored at some future point in time. And this became a -- it was something that was very frequently referred to, even in the 1990s, in terms of Serbian nationalist national belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So in essence what you're saying to the Court is that these beliefs reflect -- reappeared in the early 1990s in Bosnia-Herzegovina?
Yes, reappeared or were elaborated again as part of the Serbian historical understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you deal also briefly with the Muslims and Croats, their need to find some form of national identity within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

The Croatian understanding focused on their participation in a state which was linked with Hungary for many centuries. The Bosnian Muslims, who had converted to Islam at the time -- first century and a half after Ottoman rule, began articulating their sense of being a secular nationality comparable to the other groups in the 1960s, and so were the last of these three groups to develop a national programme and national understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move briefly to the Second World War, and again concentrating primarily on the Krajina region. Can you explain to the Judges what happened in Bosnia during the Second World War and how that is relevant to what subsequently happened in the early 1990s?

There are a number of terms or labels that were used in World War II that came to characterise the national dialogue in the 1990s. In 1941, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia were awarded by Hitler to a group of extreme Croatian nationalists, known as the Ustasha or rebels, and they established a very brutal regime in Zagreb. They engaged in atrocities and killings against Serbs, against Jews, against gypsies, and killed, at the very least, tens of thousands and probably hundreds of thousands of Serbs within the territory. And those atrocities were particularly brutal in the Bosnian Krajina. The term "Ustasha" subsequently came to be used in 1990 to refer to this form of Croatian nationalism which was perceived as a threat to Serbs. At the same time, the two resistance movements in World War II -- one was the Chetnik movement headed by a former Yugoslav royal army officer, Draza Mihajlovic, became a term in the 1990s that was used in reference to extremist Serbs who were advocating or perpetrating atrocities. Because some of the Bosnian Muslims were flattered by the inclusion in the definition of the Croatian nationality by the Ustasha, this term "Ustasha" was often used in reference to the -- say, the combination of Croatian nationalists and those -- some Bosnian Muslims who joined the Ustasha cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you state - and I can't remember the exact page for the moment - but that there was a particular Chetnik who had an idea of a Greater Serbia, and you referenced that in your report. Can you explain to the Judges what exactly is meant by Greater Serbia?

In the 19th century, each Balkan nation developed a desire to have a state which incorporated all those peoples living in neighbouring states as well. Consequently, the first nation to develop this programme was the Greeks. It was a programme for a Greater Greece. Likewise, there was a programme for a Greater Romania and Greater Bulgaria. And the Serbs, also in the process of expanding their state, developed a programme or objectives which are referred to as Greater Serbia. This really means that all Serbs in -- regardless of the political entity that they are in at the time, should ultimately be united in one state.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the ideal of Greater Serbia emerge in 1990?
Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What evidence have you come across that it was referred to, relied upon, by Serbian nationalists during that period?

Well, it is a theme that recurs many, many times in the public rhetoric and kind of closed discussions in private conferences. Not the term "Greater Serbia;" that's very rare to find. But the notion of Serbia, of a Serb state that would include all Serbs, is frequently referenced in propaganda, in public pronouncements and in closed sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, you'll be pleased to here that we have finished the historical part of Dr. Donia's evidence, and we can now move to the early 1990s and Part IV of your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, in a nutshell, what kind of society existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990?

Well, I think it's best described as a very late socialist society. After 45 years of socialism, all the republics of the former Yugoslavia were in a severe economic crisis. The social sector was large, much larger than the private sector. The government system was highly developed, and starting in the 1960s, a kind of participatory socialism had developed, which meant that most people participated in one or several social, political, economic institutions. The legal system was particularly developed and there was a good functioning -- up until late 1980s, a good functioning system of courts and extremely elaborate constitutional systems that had been in existence for really ever since the early days of the socialist state.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in the 1990s, you've already said at the beginning of your evidence that the League of Communists collapsed, and you've also identified the fact that there were leaders with nationalist tendencies who were elected in Croatia and Serbia. Can you just very briefly, for the accuracy of things, explain what happened in Slovenia and Croatia before we get to Bosnia?

Well, very briefly, Croatia and Slovenia, their parliaments issued declarations of independence on June 25th, 1991. In a brief, ten-day war -- after a brief ten-day war, the JNA, the Yugoslav National Army, left Slovenia and allowed it to go its own way. This was mediated by the European Community, which reached an agreement between the JNA and Slovenia known as the Brioni Accord, which postponed the effective date of these two declarations of independence until October of 1991. But in the meantime, a war broke out in Croatia, a war that was characterised by atrocities against civilians on both sides, and the -- I'd say deterioration of federal Yugoslavia was accelerated by this war which lasted for the rest of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The war in Croatia -- and obviously the Croatian people were on the one side. Who was against them in Croatia?

The Croatian army and its police units were opposed by the JNA, by local paramilitary groups organised by Serbs, and by some paramilitaries Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who came from Serbia to support local Serbs and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated that in that war, atrocities were committed by both sides in the war in Croatia. Did that have any bearing on the events that subsequently took place in Bosnia?

I think it had a great deal of bearing because the members of the respective kin populations in Bosnia, particularly in the Bosnian Krajina, identified with those nationalities. The Serbs of the Bosnian Krajina were eager to, in many cases, volunteer or support the cause of the Serbs in the -- that were battling the Croatian state across the border in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did the war in Croatia come to an end?

After many failed ceasefires and finally one that actually held, an agreement was signed on January 2, 1992, between the JNA and Croatia. And at the same time, there was an agreement to deploy United Nations forces to protect the -- essentially to maintain a dividing line between Croatian and Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated earlier that there were JNA units in Slovenia and in Croatia. After their withdrawal from those respective countries, what happened to those JNA units?

Most of the JNA units that had been operating or stationed in Croatia withdrew into Bosnia-Herzegovina. The prior military organisation of the JNA had placed a headquarters of a military district in Zagreb as of December, 1988. With the end of the war in Croatia, it was necessary to restructure the JNA. And so Sarajevo was elevated from a corps headquarters to the headquarters of the 2nd Military District, and at the same time, the troops of the five corps that were reporting to it were largely repositioned in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So in essence what you're saying is that the military headquarters in Sarajevo became larger because the number of military formations that was under its command increased.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's because of the withdrawal that you mentioned from Croatia.
Because of the withdrawal and the restructuring of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on the page of your report which is numbered page 31, you talk about changes in the ethnicity of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you have that page in front of you?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges what happens to the make-up -- the ethnic make-up of the manpower of the JNA in Bosnia towards the end of 1991.

Well, the JNA prior to the war in Croatia had been a genuinely multinational force. In the course of that conflict, due to the departure of many non-Serbs and the overt support for the Serbian cause that the JNA exercised in Croatia, it became essentially a Serbian army. And in the course of very late 1991, we have evidence that the Serbian President Milosevic sought to do the same thing with the JNA in Bosnia. Specifically, his colleague and advisor, presidency member Borislav Jovic reported that Milosevic ordered the JNA to take all recruits who were Bosnians and concentrate them in the Bosnian republic; and likewise, to take those recruits who were not Bosnians and transfer them to units outside of Bosnia. And later, this -- the JNA commander is quoted as saying that this was largely completed. Consequently, in the course of this transformation of the JNA, it became a -- both a more Serbian force and a more Bosnian force in the late months of 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear about this, what do you base that opinion on?

The most -- the specific information is contained in the Jovic diary, which was published a couple years ago; and there's also information to that effect in the -- a couple of the memoirs of other Yugoslav army officers from that time; and the observations of some people who were observing it from the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can move ahead to the elections in the early 1990s. Now, before those elections actually took place in former Yugoslavia - and I want you to particularly concentrate on Bosnia-Herzegovina - certain constitutional changes had to happen. Can you explain to the Judges exactly what those constitutional changes were.

Within Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were two sets of constitutional amendments that were enacted, the first in February of 1990. And those constitutional amendments stripped away some of the socialist era language and institutional suprastructure and allowed parties to be formed to compete with the League of Communists in elections yet to be scheduled. At the same time, that legislation prohibited parties based on national or religious grounds. In June of 1990, the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina ruled those prohibitions to be unconstitutional. And in the wake of that decision, national leaders rapidly formally formed and registered political parties in preparation for a -- an election in the fall. The second set of constitutional amendments were passed in -- on July 31, 1990. And those defined the nature of the offices and institutions for which people would be voting in the November election.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could remove that map, please, and put this map up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you state in your report that these constitutional changes didn't just affect the national government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but also affected the governance of the country at a local or municipal level. And this is highly relevant to this case. If you could just briefly explain to the Judges the levels of government that existed in the country and the significance of what in English is known as "the municipality" within the country.

The legislation or the constitutional amendments essentially ratified the existing situation in terms of municipalities, which in the Serbo-Croatian language -- local language is the term "opstina." And that meant that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there would be elections both at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and at the level of the municipality, the opstina. Those municipalities were essentially the basic local governing unit in Bosnia since the Ottoman times, since certainly the end of the Ottoman times. Each of those municipalities had a municipal assembly. Some of them were huge. They actually ranged in size from 27 members to 130, in the case of Banja Luka, the largest one. So in ratifying that existing situation, the Bosnian Assembly mandated the election of thousands of deputies to these municipal assemblies. They also mandated the election of 230 members of the Bosnian Assembly, divided into two chambers, and to seven members of a collective presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And just for clarification - you don't need to get up to do this - but the essentially the internal black border marks on that map identify the constituent municipality borders within Bosnia-Herzegovina as they existed, I think, in the early 1990s.
Yes. Without counting them, there should be 109 there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the borders of these municipalities always remain the same?
They were in fact changed from time to time. And the number of municipalities tended to increase, particularly during the period of socialism.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the multiparty elections. There were a number of parties, but what were the principal parties that emerged before those elections?

The three victorious parties in the election were all formed along national lines. And the first of these for the Bosnian Croats was known as the Croatian Democratic Community, HDZ. The party of the Bosnian Serbs was known as the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party. And the party of the Bosnian Muslims was known as the Party of Democratic Action, or SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just deal briefly with some of the principal actors who were involved in these political parties.

The founder -- initial founder and president of the Social Democratic Party was Radovan Karadzic. And the leader of the Muslim -- Bosnian Muslim, SDA, was Alija Izetbegovic. Each of them were from Sarjevo. Karadzic was a trained psychiatrist, and Izetbegovic kind of gained fame as a dissident who had been in prison twice in the course of the socialism. The Croatian party, HDZ, had one president early on, Davor Kavenovic [phoen], and he was replaced shortly after the formation of the party in Bosnia by Stjepan Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, these national parties, how far did they extend into the country as a whole?
Well, each of them was active in every municipality in which there were any significant numbers of the nationality living.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the -- in brief, what was the platform of these three parties? What was their manifesto?

The three parties each developed programmes in the course of the electoral campaign. Early in the campaign, they reached an agreement among them, known as the interparty agreement, not to attack one another. Consequently, there is relatively little rhetoric during the election campaign in which one party directly attacks the leader of another party. Most of the rhetoric and criticism was directed at the reformed League of Communists and the reformists that the nationalists wanted to make sure were excluded from power after the November elections. The parties, however, did disagree on one fundamental point that was regularly debated in the campaign, and that was the future constitutional relationship of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The HDZ supported a loosening of the federal relationship between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the federal state. The Serbian Democratic Party took a very firm position that the federal arrangement could not be tampered with, the federal Yugoslav state arrangement had to be maintained in exactly the fashion it was at that time. In between these two extremes was the SDA, which essentially sought to postpone a decision on this constitutional relationship until after the election. And so one finds all kinds of efforts to avoid coming to terms with this constitutional issue within the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did the Muslim party, the SDA, take this ambiguous position on the relationship of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the federal government?

Well, they were the middle party that favoured retaining Bosnia-Herzegovina as a -- an integral entity. And consequently they opposed any suggestion of partition or division and wanted to find a way that would allow everyone to be happy within the Yugoslav federation or Yugoslav arrangement on a long-term, stable basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you state in your report that in the middle of the campaign, the Serbs, the SDS, formed an organisation called the SNV. Can you explain to the Judges exactly what the SNV was and what the reaction of the existing legal structures in the country was to the establishment of that organisation.

The SDS founded the Serbian National Council in a large rally in Banja Luka in October of 1991. They did so in response to their disappointment with the failure of the constitutional amendments to provide for a third chamber of the legislature known as the Chamber of Peoples. And in establishing the SNV, they proposed that this council would exercise the same kind of role that the Chamber of Peoples would have exercised in this situation had it been approved by the Bosnian assembly before the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did the constitutional court within Bosnia-Herzegovina do when this organisation was established?
Well, the constitutional court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. It needn't be recorded. Go ahead.

utterances.text: If it's a criticism, Your Honour, it's an expert and he's written it in his report. I could ask non-leading questions but we would be here for weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Donia, where were we?
Trying to give a leading answer. The constitutional court subsequently declared this formation to be unconstitutional, on grounds that it was a -- it was usurping a state or governmental function.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What, in your expert opinion, was the significance of the formation of the SNV?

Well, in the long run, it had very little practical effect because it was not really activated much beyond that date of the 11th of October. But I think it signalled the fact that the SDS was unprepared to live with the outcome of the electoral process and insisted on some institution or institutions that would guarantee an absolute right of veto to the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there a reaction by the SDS to the decision of the constitutional court?

Well, there was no official response from the party. The party leaders responded -- some of the party leaders responded by criticising the very existence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, going back to its constitutional roots at Partisan conferences back in 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the time immediately after the national elections in Bosnia. What were the results of the elections at a national and municipal level?

The nationalist parties, HDZ, SDA and SDS, between them won an overwhelming majority of the vote. That was true in the presidency in which all seven members were members of the national parties, in the assembly in which the vast majority of elected members were from those three parties, and in almost all municipal assemblies as well. The one exception was Tuzla, in which Social Democratic -- Social Democratic Party prevailed. But in most mixed municipalities, that is municipalities with a mixed population, there was some combination of two or three national parties that commanded a majority in the local assembly, in the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, my colleague has asked me to clarify something, which is actually when the President interrupted me for asking a leading question, but in respect of the SNV, what did the constitutional court state about the formation of that organisation?
I don't have the -- that particular citation at hand, I'm sorry. I can't give it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, going back to the results of the elections -- and you've explained how it affected representation in the national and municipal level. In your report, you also refer to the division of executive positions at a national and municipal level that was actually linked to the results of the election. Can you explain to the Judges how political positions were divided between the three parties within the country?

The interparty agreement which had been made in the election campaign was elaborated and implemented in the several months following the election. This proved to be the easiest at the republican level, at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where that party that got the most votes, which was the SDA, was allowed to designate the president of the seven-person presidency, and that party chose Alija Izetbegovic. The next largest party, the SDS, was allowed to select the president of the Bosnian assembly, and that party chose Momcilo Krajisnik. And the HDZ was allowed to designate the president of the executive committee, or effectively, the Prime Minister. At the same time, the interparty agreement was applied to each municipality and became the principal -- it was almost a kind of a -- I call it a crypto-constitution because it dictated the way in which these parties would apportion positions among them within mixed municipalities. The same kind of apportionment took place in all municipalities in which there was some mixture of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did this take place in the Krajina region of Bosnia, this division of offices in the municipal governments? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

Yes, it did. It took place in a number of municipalities, which -- kind of typically, this took place in municipalities in various places of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When the local party leaders could not agree, the disputes among them would be resolved by negotiators from Sarajevo, from the party headquarters in Sarajevo, who would dictate exactly how these positions would be apportioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were, in fact, positions apportioned according to the vote within municipalities throughout Bosnia?

With -- they were in most places but often with difficulty, because the understanding of the local leaders often disagreed with what the national leadership had -- or the republican leadership of the parties had come to state. So Prijedor was one place where that disagreement was quite protracted and interfered with the formation of the assembly, municipal assembly, for a period of time.

utterances.text: Mr. President, we are now moving to a new area. I don't know if you wish me to go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I was looking at the transcript in the break and you stated at one point that Radovan Karadzic was the leader of the SDP, and I think that was a lapse on your part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said the founder of the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Founder of the SDP. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the correct position?
That's the same error I made in the paper once and it should have been SDS, both as the founder and as the president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if we can go to page 41 of your report, and there is a subtitle within the body of the report that states "Regionalisation." Can you explain to the Judges what the term "regionalisation" meant within the context of Bosnia in 1990 and 1991?

"Regionalisation" was a term for a campaign that was undertaken, principally by the SDS, to establish areas, territories of the country, under single national and one-party political domination. The term was used in public discussions, in press discussions, and also in party councils of the SDS. It referred specifically to three strategies that were used in varying situations to accomplish this territorial domination. The first was the formation of regional associations of municipalities which had Serb majority populations, which were interposed between the municipal level and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second strategy was to rearrange the organisation of municipalities such that Serbian majority parts of municipalities would either be broken off as new municipalities or joined with other municipalities that already had a Serb majority. And the third strategy to which this concept referred was to create a kind of a shadow assembly which was called either a Serbian Assembly or a Serbian Municipality, which was a set of parallel institutions to the government of that particular municipality. Those are the three strategies that made up the concept of "regionalisation" throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, principally in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina ever allow for regionalisation?

The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina did allow for regional associations of municipalities to be formed for certain limited purposes, defined purposes: for economic cooperation, for cultural and informational cooperation. This is a concept somewhat like a school district or a water district. And in fact, as of 1989/1990, there were two associations of municipalities in existence in the Bosnian Krajina area. The first was called the Bihac Municipal Association, and the other was called the Banja Luka Association of Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any provision within the constitution for municipalities to be associated on the basis of nationality?
There was no such provision in the constitution, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, concentrating specifically on the Krajina area that is relevant to this case, can you explain to the Judges how regionalisation took place in that area? Pausing for a moment just to make matters clear, so that we're absolutely fair. Did the Muslims and Croats engage in regionalisation?

Yes, both did. The HDZ did not in the first instance after the election engage in regionalisation. But starting in November of 1991, it promoted regional associations, the most important of which was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Muslims were generally opposed to regionalisation, but in a few selected cases, organised municipalities or institutions, largely in response to situations in which they were trying to avoid the consequences of regionalisation, particularly by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When did the Muslims engage in regionalisation?

Well, there was a combined Croat-Muslim, very short-lived, regionalisation effort in the Sarajevo municipality of Ilidza. And there was also an effort to -- organisation of a Muslim municipality in Banja Luka. I believe there were one or two others in selected parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can't give you specific locations where that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, going back to my original question, before I paused. Regionalisation in the Krajina area, did regionalisation take place there?

Regionalisation really began in the Bosnian Krajina area in 1991. The SDS announced in April of 1991 -- a SDS spokesman announced at a press conference that the party leadership had been discussing and planning regionalisation since starting in January of 1991. And in fact, in April of 1991, the newspaper -- daily newspaper in Banja Luka, Glas, or "voice," ran a series of articles which were interviews with local political leaders and intellectuals who advocated the development of a regional approach in response to alleged neglect of the region from Sarajevo, from the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And on 10th, 11th, and 12th of April, 1991, the Serbian assemblies of roughly ten municipalities proclaimed themselves or issued decisions saying that they had joined the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, which became known by its acronym in the local language of ZOBK. These declarations were publicised in -- they were covered in Glas newspaper, and the proclamations evoked some rather forceful responses from leaders of other parties, other than the SDS. May I just -- if I may, Mr. President, I'd like to disclose that the Office of the Prosecutor invited me to review a limited set of documents on which some of these conclusions are based. And those documents consisted of the minutes and conclusions of the ZOBK and the Krajina and also the transcripts of minutes of the Bosnian Serb Assembly and some related documents to these. In addition, I've looked at a great deal of periodical press and other documentation. I just would like to state that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And as we're about to move into documents, I can confirm, Mr. President, that the Defence have all of the documents, except for one which we're not going to use, which they now have, which Dr. Donia has looked at to compile his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could just take you back for a moment, Dr. Donia, you've moved ahead to April of 1991 and I want to just go back to January for a moment. The campaign to establish the ZOBK, when did it begin?

The SDS announced in April that the campaign, or the plans, the discussion, had begun in January of 1991. Now, this was in fact a discussion that had been -- the general concept of regionalisation had been discussed for some time beforehand, and it was discussed intensively in the press starting in March of 1991, but there was no specific organisational prescription or recommendation that came out of this discussion at that time. The first indication of a specific organisation really arose on 10 April, 1991, when the first of these municipalities announced their affiliation or membership in the ZOBK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you cite two various reasons that were given by the SDS as to why this regionalisation was taking place, that there had been a lack of investment in the region by the central government in Sarajevo. Were, in your opinion, the reasons that were given for regionalisation in the Krajina justified?

The rhetoric, the language that was used, alleged great discrimination, concentration of wealth in Sarajevo and discrimination against this impoverished region. There actually was no evidence presented to suggest any significant difference in the economic development levels in this entire campaign, that I've seen. And in fact, I've quoted Dr. Dusko Jaksic as noting that there really was no statistical evidence in support of this. I do believe that there was a widespread perception of that, in part because all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and for that matter Yugoslavia, was at this time in a steep economic decline and it was very easy to believe that others were doing better than one's particular region. But there doesn't seem to be much of a -- evidence, really, that the Bosnian Krajina was in worse shape than other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, before we move to the documents, a last point, and if you could turn to page 42 of your report, to the paragraph dealing with a conversation between Mirko Pejanovic and Radovan Karadzic in August 1990. Now, I know we are dealing specifically with regionalisation in the Bosnian Krajina but if you could explain the relevance of this conversation between these two men in August of 1992, regionalisation throughout the country, including the Krajina?

August of 1990, before the election, and Mirko Pejanovic, who was at that time president of the political party that had emerged from the socialist alliance, was then seeking to get all parties contending in the election to agree to a common platform, support the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina and democratic change. And this was a coincidental conversation that he reports in his memoirs which suggests that from the early days of the party, regionalisation, that is the creation of Serbian municipalities, was very much on the mind and in the plans of the party leadership.
